text: What would happen if you got lost alone in the Amazon rainforest?
It starts with a few steps off the trail. You turn around... and the trail is gone.
Every direction looks the same. The canopy hides the sun, and your phone has no signal.
Experts say that when you're lost, you should stop and stay put. But that only works if someone knows where you are. And nobody does.
So you walk. Without the sun or landmarks, people often walk in circles without realizing it.
It's over thirty degrees, and the air is so humid your sweat barely evaporates. You're soaking wet, but your body can't cool down.
You find a stream. But untreated, this water can carry parasites and bacteria, and diarrhea would drain your body even faster.
Then the afternoon rain arrives. Rainwater is one of the safest drinks out here, so you catch every drop you can.
And the stream gives you a plan. Small streams flow into bigger rivers, and rivers are where people live. So you follow it downstream.
Night falls fast. Under the canopy, it's pitch black, and the forest only gets louder. Soaked to the skin, you shiver, even in the tropics.
By day three, insect bites cover your skin, and a small cut on your arm is red and swollen. In this heat, wounds can get infected in days.
Then you nearly step on a fer-de-lance, the snake behind most bites in the Amazon. You freeze, back away slowly, and give it space.
say: Then you nearly step on a fair-duh-lance, the snake behind most bites in the Amazon. You freeze, back away slowly, and give it space.

text: You're starving, but unknown berries and mushrooms could poison you. You can last weeks without food. Water is what keeps you alive.
On day five, the stream opens onto a wide river. And then you hear it... an engine.
In 1971, after a plane crash, seventeen-year-old Juliane Koepcke survived eleven days alone in the Amazon, by doing exactly this. Following the water.
